finding: Reviewed twelve foundational identification, transport, IV and proximal primary papers against the exact 626-page reader. No essential manuscript defect found in these scopes.
next_action: Continue Q2 with DML, treatment heterogeneity and longitudinal primary papers, then remaining discovery, LLM, software/commercial and public-data records; resume semantic-review-11.json. Preserve theorem assumptions and negative findings.

records.finding: Structural assignments and autonomous replacement, d-separation, model-class identification, truncated factorization and sufficient back-door adjustment match the primary definitions and theorem. The IV graph alone does not identify the unrestricted ATE. All nine citation contexts preserve these distinctions; project examples and controlled likelihood compositions are not attributed as new theorems of the source.

DAG equivalence requires the same skeleton and unshielded colliders; front-door adjustment uses the stated support and mediator restrictions. Restricted additive-noise identification excludes reversible cases. Granger prediction depends on its information set, causal sufficiency and timing. All five manuscript contexts keep these limitations.

Figure 2 and the C-forest/hedge definitions support the manuscript district recursion and bow obstruction. Figure 3 and Theorems 7-8 support the conditional rescue despite an unidentified joint query. The traced front-door kernel p(a)p(y|a,m) and the observation/action exchange use the correct graph modification. No general counterfactual identification or implemented ID backend is inferred from the theorem.

Node splitting, modularity and single-world factorization match the manuscript. FFRCISTG is distinguished from the stronger independent-error model. Neither the joint pair of incompatible potential outcomes nor a natural direct effect is obtained merely from a single-world graph.

Definitions 1-4 and Theorem 5 require amenability, forbidden-set avoidance and blocking proper definite-status noncausal paths across compatible models. The manuscript limits its completeness statement to adjustment and does not turn failed adjustment into a general nonidentification certificate.

Selection diagrams mark permitted mechanism changes. Theorem 2 and Corollary 1 justify pretreatment S-admissible reweighting; source support and common intervention/outcome meanings remain necessary. The proxy-shift example correctly rejects automatic reweighting, and the later pooled-sample gradient is clearly project work.

Assumption 1 fixes a common linear response and noise law; Proposition 1 requires interventions that preserve the outcome mechanism. Theorem 1 controls false inclusion by intersection of nonrejected sets, not discovery of every parent. The manuscript proof, candidate-set condition, screening caveat and refusal to treat arbitrary calendar splits as valid environments match these premises.

Definition 4.9 constructs equilibrium equations, Theorem 4.11 maps convergent solutions into them, and Theorem 4.18 concerns steady interventions and model equilibration. The manuscript separately requires actual convergence and does not infer uniqueness or convergence merely by setting derivatives to zero.

The primary structural IV example distinguishes endogenous receipt from assignment. Equation 9 and Table 1 yield complier-minus-defier weighting; exclusion, nonzero first stage and monotonicity yield Proposition 1 LATE. Manuscript adds assignment independence for the observed Wald ratio and does not generalize the complier target to the population ATE.

The 2002 working-paper bytes support joint instrument/disturbance independence, strict monotonicity in latent rank, control-rank recovery and conditional response identification on observed support. Theorem 2 needs additional support for the marginal structural response. The manuscript stratifies by observed covariates explicitly and distinguishes rank monotonicity from binary IV monotonicity.

Finite-proxy factorization and the continuous bridge theorem require the proxy exclusions plus rank or latent completeness. Theorem 1 permits nonunique bridge solutions while identifying their causal average. The manuscript keeps latent completeness, bridge existence and observable uniqueness separate; the finite financial calculation is a labeled reconstruction.

Assumptions 4-6 and Theorem 3 support the mean outcome-bridge formula; treatment-bridge identification uses its counterpart assumptions. The source restricts local efficiency to the uniquely identified intersection model. Assumptions 2-3 and Theorem 2 require consistency and projected-error/ill-posedness control, which the manuscript retains rather than copying ordinary AIPW rates.
